title: Culture Formatting and Request Culture Providers
description: Configure culture-specific formatting for dates, numbers, and currency, and understand how ASP.NET Core detects the user's preferred culture.

terms.definition: Controls formatting for dates, numbers, and currencies. Example: en-US formats dates as MM/dd/yyyy and uses $ for currency; fr-FR uses dd/MM/yyyy and €.
Controls which resource file is loaded for translated strings. Usually set to the same value as Culture but can differ if you want English formatting with French strings.
A strategy that inspects each incoming HTTP request to determine the user's preferred culture. ASP.NET Core tries providers in order until one succeeds.
Reads culture and ui-culture from URL query string parameters (e.g., ?culture=fr&ui-culture=fr). Best for demos and manual testing.
Reads culture from an ASP.NET Core authentication cookie. The culture persists across requests without appearing in the URL. Best for user preferences.
Reads the Accept-Language header sent by the browser, which reflects the user's OS or browser language settings. Best as a fallback.

data.text: Globalization vs Localization Recap

Globalization is about designing your app to support many cultures — dates, numbers, currencies, and calendars all change based on culture. Localization is about providing the actual translated content (strings) for each culture. Both are handled together through the request localization middleware.

data.title: Culture vs UICulture at a glance
data.text: Culture affects how numbers, dates, and currencies are formatted. UICulture determines which resource file is loaded for translated strings. Setting both to 'fr' gives you French formatting AND French strings.
Step 1 — Complete Configuration in Program.cs
Before you can format culture-specific content, the middleware pipeline needs to know which cultures to support. Here is the complete setup:

data.title: Program.cs — full localization setup
data.content: Complete Program.cs configuration supporting English, French, and Spanish with cookie and query-string culture providers.

data.text: Step 2 — Display Culture-Dependent Values in a View
Once the middleware sets the culture, .NET automatically formats dates, numbers, and currencies. Display them in a view to show the difference:

data.title: Views/Home/CultureDemo.cshtml
data.content: A view that displays culture-sensitive values: date, currency, and number formatting change automatically based on ?culture=.

data.text: Step 3 — Use QueryStringRequestCultureProvider
The simplest provider for testing is the query string provider. It reads `?culture=xx&ui-culture=xx` from the URL. This is the default first provider, so it works without any extra configuration.

data.title: URL examples
data.content: The same view renders differently depending on the query string culture parameter.
data.code:
# English (default)
https://localhost:5001/Home/CultureDemo

# French — date, currency, and number format all switch
https://localhost:5001/Home/CultureDemo?culture=fr-FR&ui-culture=fr-FR

# Spanish
https://localhost:5001/Home/CultureDemo?culture=es-ES&ui-culture=es-ES

data.title: Culture and ui-culture can differ
data.text: You can set ?culture=en-US&ui-culture=fr to get English date/number formatting but French resource strings. This is useful for bilingual regions.
Step 4 — Use CookieRequestCultureProvider
For production apps, storing the user's preference in a cookie is better than a query string — it persists across requests without polluting URLs. The cookie name is `.AspNetCore.Culture` by default.

data.title: Controllers/HomeController.cs — set culture cookie
data.content: An action that writes the user's culture choice into a cookie that persists for one month.

data.title: Culture cookie form — add to your layout or view
data.content: A dropdown that POSTs to SetLanguage without changing the URL.
data.code: <form asp-controller="Home" asp-action="SetLanguage" method="post" id="cultureForm" class="d-inline"> <input type="hidden" name="returnUrl" value="@Context.Request.Path" /> <label>Language:</label> <select name="culture" onchange="this.form.submit()" class="form-select d-inline-block w-auto"> <option value="en-US" selected="@(CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture.Name == \"en-US\")">English</option> <option value="fr-FR" selected="@(CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture.Name == \"fr-FR\")">Français</option> <option value="es-ES" selected="@(CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture.Name == \"es-ES\")">Español</option> </select> </form>

data.text: Step 5 — Use AcceptLanguageHeaderRequestCultureProvider
This provider reads the `Accept-Language` header sent by the browser, which reflects the user's OS or browser language preference. It requires no UI — just set your browser language and reload.

data.title: How to test the Accept-Language header
data.text: In Chrome: Settings → Advanced → Languages → move French to the top. In Edge: Settings → Languages. In Firefox: Options → General → Language. Then clear the culture cookie and reload the page.
Step 6 — Build a Custom Request Culture Provider
You can add your own culture provider for scenarios not covered by the built-in providers. A common pattern is extracting the culture from the URL path, e.g. `/fr/Home/Index`.

data.title: Program.cs — custom URL segment culture provider
data.content: A CustomRequestCultureProvider that reads the first URL segment as the culture code.

data.title: Resulting URLs
data.content: With the custom provider, the culture is the first path segment — no query string needed.
data.code:
# English (default)
https://localhost:5001/Home/Index

# French — first segment 'fr' is the culture
https://localhost:5001/fr/Home/Index

# Spanish
https://localhost:5001/es/Home/Index

data.title: Use AddInitialRequestCultureProvider for URL-based culture
data.text: AddInitialRequestCultureProvider inserts your provider at the front of the list, so it runs before the query string, cookie, and header providers. This is essential for URL segment culture detection.
Step 7 — Custom Provider from a Database
For authenticated users, you may want to store their preferred culture in a database. A custom provider can read the user's profile on every request:

data.title: Custom provider reading from UserManager
data.content: A custom RequestCultureProvider that fetches the logged-in user's culture from the database.

data.title: Register the database provider
data.text: Register UserCultureProvider as a scoped service and add it to RequestCultureProviders before the built-in providers so it takes priority for logged-in users.

data.caption: RequestCultureProviders are tried in order — first successful result wins
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[Incoming HTTP Request] --> B[Localization Middleware]
    B --> C[Provider 1: QueryString]
    C -->|?culture=fr found| D[Set Culture = fr]
    C -->|not found| E[Provider 2: Cookie]
    E -->|cookie found| D
    E -->|not found| F[Provider 3: Browser Header]
    F -->|Accept-Language found| D
    F -->|not found| G[Use Default: en-US]
    D --> H[Request processed with culture set]
    G --> H

cards.title: QueryStringRequestCultureProvider
cards.description: Reads ?culture=fr&ui-culture=fr from the URL. Simple, explicit, but clutters URLs.
pros: Easy to test — just change the URL
cons: Culture appears in URL — not SEO friendly
Not persistent across page reloads without the parameter

cards.title: CookieRequestCultureProvider
cards.description: Stores culture in a .AspNetCore.Culture cookie. Persists across the whole site visit.
cons: Requires a form or JS to set the cookie

cards.title: AcceptLanguageHeaderRequestCultureProvider
cards.description: Reads the browser's Accept-Language header automatically. No UI needed.
cons: User cannot override without changing browser settings
Browser setting may not match user's actual preference

cards.title: Custom RequestCultureProvider
cards.description: Your own implementation — read culture from URL segments, a database, a JWT claim, etc.
pros: Fully flexible — read culture from anywhere
Can combine with user profile data
cons: Must handle edge cases (invalid culture, fallbacks)

data.title: Exercise: Build a Culture-Aware Dashboard
data.description: Apply all three providers to build a dashboard that respects user culture preferences.
steps: Configure Program.cs with en-US, fr-FR, and es-ES cultures.
Set RequestCultureProviders to [QueryString, Cookie, AcceptLanguageHeader] in that order.
Create a Dashboard view that shows: current date, price (€12,345.67), percentage (15.5%), and today's day name.
Add a culture dropdown form that sets the culture via cookie (POST to SetLanguage).
Add a link that uses query string to switch to French: /Dashboard?culture=fr-FR&ui-culture=fr-FR.
Change your browser's preferred language to Spanish, clear the cookie, and confirm the dashboard shows Spanish values.
Add a custom URL provider that reads culture from the first path segment (/fr/Dashboard).
data.expectedOutcome: A dashboard that correctly applies French or Spanish formatting from any of the three providers, and falls back to English when no provider matches.

items.hint: Include all cultures you plan to support

items.text: DefaultRequestCulture is set to your fallback culture
items.hint: Usually your primary language, e.g. en-US
Most specific provider first (cookie), most general last (header)

items.text: Culture switcher cookie has IsEssential = true
items.hint: Required for GDPR compliance if consent is needed

items.text: Custom providers return null on failure (not throw)
items.hint: Returning null lets the next provider try

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Culture controls date/number/currency formatting; UICulture controls which resource file is loaded.
ASP.NET Core tries RequestCultureProviders in order — first match wins.
QueryStringRequestCultureProvider is best for testing; CookieRequestCultureProvider is best for production.
AcceptLanguageHeaderRequestCultureProvider provides automatic browser-based detection as a fallback.
Use AddInitialRequestCultureProvider to add a custom provider that runs before built-in providers.
A custom provider can read culture from URL segments, a database, or any other source.
data.takeaway: Understanding culture providers is the key to a polished multilingual experience. Combine them in order of specificity for the best user experience.

items.question: What is the correct order for RequestCultureProviders?
items.answer: Put the most explicit provider first. The recommended order is: QueryString (user choice via URL), Cookie (user choice persisted), AcceptLanguageHeader (browser default). This way, an explicit user choice always overrides the browser setting.

items.question: Why does my date still show in English even with ?culture=fr?
items.answer: Make sure UseRequestLocalization is before UseRouting, not after. Also confirm the fr-FR culture is in SupportedCultures — if you only registered 'fr' but are requesting 'fr-FR', the provider won't match.

items.question: Can I use a URL segment like /fr/ instead of ?culture=fr?
items.answer: Yes — use a CustomRequestCultureProvider with AddInitialRequestCultureProvider. The provider reads the first URL segment and returns a ProviderCultureResult. See the custom provider example in this lesson.

items.question: How do I store the user's preferred culture in the database?
items.answer: Create a class that inherits RequestCultureProvider, override DetermineProviderCultureResult to query your user store, and add it to the providers list. The exercise in Lesson 2 on custom providers shows a complete example.
